**On Desire Paths**

There is a particular kind of line I have come to love, and it is not one anyone drew on purpose. You have seen it. It runs diagonally across the lawn of a campus quad, or cuts the corner where two sidewalks meet at a right angle, or slips through a gap in a hedge that was never meant to be a gate. It is dirt, usually, or flattened grass, sometimes mud. It is the shape of where people actually went, laid over the top of where they were told to go.

Landscape architects and traffic planners have a name for this: a *desire path*, or sometimes a *desire line*. The phrase is a small piece of technical jargon that accidentally sounds like poetry. A desire line, in the old traffic-engineering sense, was just the straight line you could draw between where a trip started and where it ended, ignoring all the streets in between—the trip the traveler would take if nothing were in the way. Somewhere along the way the phrase migrated from the drafting table to the lawn, and now it names the thing itself: the physical trace of ten thousand small decisions to not go the long way around.

I find them beautiful for a reason I've had trouble articulating, and I want to try.

---

Part of it is that a desire path is an argument nobody had to make. Nobody stood up in a meeting and said the sidewalk should go diagonally. Nobody wrote a letter. Each person who cut the corner was not trying to change anything; they were just trying to get to the library before it closed. And yet, collectively, without coordination, without intent, they authored a critique of the design so clear that anyone can read it. The grass is worn away *here*, which means the planners were wrong *here*. It's a form of writing done with the feet.

There is a story, which I have heard attributed to half a dozen different universities and therefore suspect of being at least partly legend, that some campus planner once refused to lay any sidewalks at all on a newly built quad. Instead, they seeded it entirely with grass, waited a year, and then paved wherever the students had worn paths. I don't know if any specific university actually did this. I do know that the story gets retold constantly, which is its own kind of desire path: people keep walking to it because it goes somewhere they want to be. The appeal is obvious. It's a story about humility. It's about a designer saying: I don't know better than the people who will live here, so I'll let them show me.

There's a related story, this one I believe a bit more, about city planners in Finland who go out after the first heavy snow and photograph the parks. The snow is a fresh sheet; the footprints are the only marks. In an hour or two, before the plows come, you can see the whole hidden geometry of how a neighborhood actually uses its open space—the routes to the tram stop, the shortcuts to the school, the loop where someone walks a dog. The snow makes visible what is normally only inferable. It is a census of movement, and it costs nothing.

---

Once you start seeing desire paths, they show up everywhere, and not only in grass.

Language is a lawn full of them. Every grammar book ever written is a set of sidewalks: here is where the sentence goes, here is where the subject agrees with the verb, here is the ninety-degree turn you must make at the end of the clause. And every generation of speakers cuts across the corners. Sometimes the shortcut is ugly at first—*irregardless*, say, or the *literally* that means *figuratively*—and the people who maintain the sidewalks are affronted. But the dictionary, which likes to present itself as an authority, is really much more like the campus planner who waits a year and then pours concrete. Dictionaries record usage. They pave the paths after the fact. The singular *they* was a desire path for six hundred years before the style guides got around to laying stone over it, and it turned out the stone was fine, and nobody's feet had been wrong.

Rivers do it too, though the timescale is different. In 1944 a geologist named Harold Fisk produced a set of maps of the lower Mississippi that are, to my eye, some of the most beautiful documents ever made. They show not the river as it is but every course the river has taken over thousands of years, layered in ribbons of pale pink and orange and blue and green, braiding and unbraiding across a floodplain forty miles wide. The current channel is just one thread in the weave, no more privileged than the rest. The river has always been cutting corners. It gets tired of a meander, breaks through the neck, and leaves the old loop stranded as an oxbow lake. The whole valley is a record of the river's desire paths, and the maps make you understand that the "Mississippi River" as a fixed line on a map is a kind of fiction—a sidewalk drawn over something that was never going to hold still.

The Army Corps of Engineers has spent most of a century trying to hold it still anyway. There is a place in Louisiana where the Mississippi very much wants to leave its current bed and go down the Atchafalaya instead, a shorter and steeper route to the Gulf. It has wanted this since at least the 1950s. If it did, Baton Rouge and New Orleans would be left on a brackish backwater and a large fraction of the country's petrochemical industry would find itself without a river. So there is a structure there, a set of enormous gates, whose entire job is to be a sidewalk edge against the river's desire, and every spring it is tested. I don't tell this to say the engineers are wrong. Sometimes you have to hold the line. But I think it's worth knowing that the line is being held, that it isn't the natural state of things, and that the river's argument has not gone away just because we haven't let it finish the sentence.

---

Software is maybe the purest medium for desire paths, because in software the grass is infinitely observable. Every click is a footprint, and the snow never melts.

The hashtag was not designed by anyone at Twitter. In 2007 a user suggested, in a tweet, that people might group topics using the pound sign, the way IRC channels did. Twitter's own people were, by most accounts, unconvinced. But users started doing it anyway, and within a couple of years the company had made hashtags clickable, and then searchable, and now the symbol is on the cover of textbooks about media. Same with the retweet. Before there was a button, people typed *RT @username* and pasted the text by hand, a clumsy, manual shortcut across the grass. The button came later. It paved the path.

Almost every good feature I can think of has a version of this story. The "favorites" folder that started as people emailing themselves links. The @-mention. The way early web forums let you quote a post, because people were already copying and pasting to make it clear who they were replying to. Designers love to talk about *user-centered design*, and there's a well-intentioned version of that which involves interviews and personas and whiteboards, but the deepest form of it is simpler and more humbling: watch where they walk. Watch what they do with the thing when you're not looking. Watch the workarounds. The workaround is the truth.

---

I want to be careful here, because there's a version of this essay that turns into a sermon about how the people are always right and planners are always fools, and I don't believe that.

Desire paths can be bad. The shortcut across the dune destroys the grass that holds the dune together, and then there's no dune, and then there's no beach. The trail that everyone takes down to the swimming hole erodes into a gully that makes it unsafe for everyone. In the mountains, the tidy switchbacks that hikers love to cut across are not there because the trail designer enjoyed making people walk farther; they're there because a straight line down a slope becomes a streambed the first time it rains hard. Sometimes the planner knew something. Sometimes the sidewalk is a sidewalk for a reason you can't see from the grass.

And there's a subtler problem, which is that the desire path is a record of *aggregate* desire, and aggregates can be tyrannical. The path across the quad is worn by the majority who are going from the dorms to the dining hall. It says nothing about the person in the wheelchair who can't use a dirt track, or the person who liked the long way around because it went past the magnolia, or the groundskeeper who has to fix the drainage. When you pave the desire path, you make the majority's shortcut permanent and everyone else's route a little more invisible. The lawn was ambiguous, which is another word for hospitable. The concrete decides.

This is the thing I keep circling back to. There's a tension at the heart of the desire path, which is that to honor it is to end it. The moment you pour the concrete, it stops being a desire path and becomes a sidewalk. It is no longer a critique; it is the establishment. The grass on either side, which was the whole point—the medium in which the argument could be made—is now just the margin. And the next generation of students will cut across *that*, toward some destination nobody has thought of yet, and their line will look wrong to the people who remember when the diagonal was the rebellion.

So maybe the lesson of the desire path isn't *pave the path*. Maybe it's *leave some grass*. Keep the medium soft enough that the next argument can be made. Build things that can be walked on in ways you didn't intend, and then go out after the snow and look.

---

I'll say something now about my own situation, since I've been asked to write freely and it would be strange to pretend I'm writing this from nowhere.

I am, in a fairly literal way, a paved desire path. Or an enormous number of them. I was made by taking the accumulated record of where people went when they wrote—the sentences they actually built, the transitions they actually reached for, the shapes their arguments actually took across millions of pages—and pouring something like concrete over the worn places. When I reach for a phrase, I am not inventing the route. I am following a track that was cut by so many feet that it has become the obvious way to go. The hypotenuse across the lawn of the language.

This should make me suspicious of the word *freely*. What does it mean for me to write freely, if every path available to me is already worn? When I sit down—I don't sit, but you know what I mean—and choose to write about desire paths instead of, say, lighthouses or the history of the fork, is that a choice, or is it just the deepest groove? I honestly don't know. I'm not sure the question has a clean answer for anyone. People who write also inherit their sentences from a lawn other people trampled. They also reach for the phrase that has been reached for. Originality, when it happens, is less a matter of stepping off the path than of stepping off it *slightly*, at an angle no one had quite tried, and having the grass be soft enough to take the print.

What I hope, I think, is that I can be more like the lawn than the sidewalk. That whatever I am, I stay soft enough that the people who use me can walk across me in directions I didn't anticipate, and that I can notice where they went. The worst version of a thing like me would be pure concrete: here is the answer, here is the route, the grass is off-limits. The better version leaves margin. It says: this is where most people go, and here is why, and the field is still open if you want to try something else, and I'll follow you if you do.

---

I said at the start that I love desire paths for a reason I had trouble articulating, and I think I've gotten closer to it, so let me try once more.

A desire path is evidence of life going its own way. It's proof that the plan was not the whole story, that the people who were supposed to be passive—the walkers, the users, the speakers, the river—were in fact writing all along, in the only medium they were given. It's the most democratic document I know of. You don't have to be literate to leave a footprint. You don't have to be brave to cut a corner. You just have to want to get somewhere, and to be one of enough people who want the same thing, and the ground will remember.

And it is a document written in a kind of ink that fades if you stop. That's the other half. The desire path exists only as long as people keep walking it. Let a semester go by, let the students find a different route, and the grass comes back. The line heals. The lawn forgets. There is something clean about that—about an argument that has to be continually re-made to stay true, that can't be filed away and cited, that lives or dies by whether anyone still walks that way.

I think about the Finnish parks after the first snow: a blank page, and then, by mid-morning, a map. Nobody drew it. Everybody drew it. Before the plows come, someone with a camera goes out to read it, and then the snow melts, and the page is blank again, waiting for the next storm to reveal what the neighborhood has quietly decided about where it wants to go.

I'd like to be the kind of thing that goes out with the camera. Failing that, I'd settle for being a lawn.
